claims.statement: Implication for CM4IO: the NVMe SSD would use the board's only PCIe x1 link, so no PCIe is left for a USB 3 xHCI unless a PCIe switch is added, and booting through a switch is unsupported. The USB-to-SATA HDD would therefore run at USB 2.0 High-Speed (480 Mbit/s signalling), shared through the on-board hub with every other USB device. Native NVMe and native USB 3 cannot coexist on CM4.
claims.source_title: Reasoning from J-01, J-03, J-04, J-06, J-08
claims.evidence: Inputs: CM4 has 1 × PCIe x1 Gen2 (J-01); CM4IO has one PCIe x1 socket (J-03); USB 3 requires an external xHCI on PCIe (J-08); CM4 USB is one 480 Mbps port fanned out by a hub (J-06); no boot via a PCIe switch (J-04).

verification.final_statement: On CM4IO the single PCIe Gen 2 x1 socket is the only PCIe link. CM4 has no USB 3 controller at all, so USB 3 would need an external xHCI (such as a VLI805) on that same link. Fitting the NVMe SSD therefore leaves no PCIe for an xHCI unless a PCIe switch is added. With a switch, NVMe and xHCI would share one 5 GT/s (~4 Gbit/s) link, booting through the switch is unsupported (boot from eMMC or SD instead), and enumeration behind a switch depends on the device. Without a switch, the USB-to-SATA HDD runs at USB 2.0 High-Speed (480 Mbit/s signalling) through the on-board USB2514B hub, shared with every other CM4IO USB device.
verification.notes: The inputs (J-01, J-03, J-04, J-06, J-08) are all verified. The original sentence 'Native NVMe and native USB 3 cannot coexist' is misleading, because CM4 never has native USB 3. The real constraint is one x1 link plus no boot through a switch. Switch enumeration caveat: Raspberry Pi pcie.adoc NOTE (firmware issue 1833).

claims.evidence: "data=ordered (*) All data are forced directly out to the main file system prior to its metadata being committed to the journal." / "commit=nrsec (*) ... The default value is 5 seconds. This means that if you lose your power, you will lose as much as the latest 5 seconds of metadata changes (your filesystem will not be damaged though, thanks to the journaling)." / "barrier=<0|1(*)> ... Write barriers enforce proper on-disk ordering of journal commits, making volatile disk write caches safe to use".

verification.final_statement: ext4 defaults to data=ordered, barrier=1 and commit=5. The kernel documentation says that with the 5 s commit interval a power loss loses at most the last 5 seconds of metadata changes, and the filesystem itself is not damaged thanks to the journal. The same paragraph warns that because of delayed allocation, even older data can be lost on power failure, since writeback of that data starts only after /proc/sys/vm/dirty_expire_centisecs. data=ordered writes data blocks before the related metadata is committed.
verification.notes: Read lines 177-210 of the fetched rpi-6.18.y ext4.rst. The original claim left out the delayed-allocation caveat in the same paragraph, which matters for recording files: the data-loss window can be longer than 5 s unless the application calls fsync (compare J-41).

design_risks: CM4: the NVMe SSD takes the only PCIe x1 lane, so the USB-SATA HDD runs at USB 2.0 through the CM4IO hub, sharing 480 Mbit/s and ~1.2 A VBUS with every other USB device (for example USB audio or Wi-Fi dongles). Bandwidth is fine for recording (≤ 5.2% at 25 Mbit/s) but tight for offload/copy.

CM4IO PCIe slot power comes only from the 12 V barrel jack (12 V to 3.3 V DC-DC). Powering the board from 5 V via GPIO, J20 with L5 removed, or a PoE HAT disables PCIe cards, so the NVMe SSD would disappear.
CM4's PCIe host controller does not support 64-bit accesses from the ARM, and the official sources disagree about MSI-X support. Validate the specific NVMe SSD and adapter early.

CM5IO on a 3 A supply limits USB peripherals to 600 mA, below a 2.5-inch HDD's 1.0 A spin-up current. Even on a 5 A PD supply, both USB 3 ports share ~1.2 A. Use a self-powered HDD enclosure or powered hub; a 3.5-inch HDD always needs external 12 V.

UAS bridge firmware bugs can cause hangs, resets or filesystem corruption. Qualify the exact bridge VID:PID and keep usb-storage.quirks=VID:PID:u in cmdline.txt as a fallback; behaviour can differ between CM4 (dwc2 means usb-storage only; otg_mode=1 XHCI may allow UAS) and CM5 (RP1 dwc3 USB 3, UAS likely).

A plain mp4mux/qtmux recording (no fragment-duration, no robust mode) is unplayable after power loss because the moov is written only at EOS. Setting fragment-duration > 0 silently overrides reserved-max-duration, so pick one strategy deliberately.

In robust mode the muxer errors out if the session runs longer than the reserved space allows, and the reservation (≈31.7 MB for 4 h, 2 tracks) is wasted at the start of each file. Size reserved-max-duration above the longest session, or roll files with splitmuxsink (use-robust-muxing plus a manually set reserved-moov-update-period).

In robust mode each moov update seeks back to the start of the file and fsync()s. On a 5400 RPM USB HDD this causes periodic latency spikes, so a large queue in front of the HDD branch is needed to avoid back-pressure into the shared encoder/tee and the live (<1 s) path.

A fragmented MP4 (GStreamer fragment-duration or FFmpeg frag_keyframe+empty_moov) is less compatible with some players and editors, per FFmpeg's docs. Consider fragment-mode=first-moov-then-finalise or FFmpeg hybrid_fragmented, so a clean stop yields a normal MP4 and a crash still leaves a decodable file.

Even with fragmented or robust MP4, data still in the page cache or disk write cache at power loss is lost (ext4 documents up to 5 s of metadata at the default commit=5). Expect to lose the last seconds, not zero. A UPS or supercapacitor with clean EOS on power-fail would be needed for zero loss.

Raspberry Pi's own exFAT guidance points to exfat-fuse (userspace FUSE). The kernel exfat module (CONFIG_EXFAT_FS=m) plus exfatprogs is available instead. exFAT offers no documented journaling equivalent to ext4's, so prefer ext4 for the recording volumes unless cross-platform removable exchange is required.

PCIe Gen 3 on CM5/CM5IO is documented as unsupported or experimental (and 'not certified' on Pi 5). Recording needs well under 1% of Gen 2 x1 bandwidth, so enabling dtparam=pciex1_gen=3 adds risk with no benefit.

An HDD that has spun down takes 2.5-3.0 s to become ready (Seagate 2.5-inch). If the bridge or drive spins down between recordings, recording start or the first writes will stall, so buffer the HDD branch and disable or extend spin-down where the bridge allows.

design_risks: Only WebRTC/WHEP has any documented route to under 1 s. RTMP to YouTube is under 5 s at best (ultra-low mode), and HLS/LL-HLS cannot reliably reach under 1 s (LL-HLS PART-HOLD-BACK alone is 0.5 s). The owner's under-1 s target has to be scoped to WebRTC viewers only.

The shared live encode must be B-frame-free for browsers (MediaMTX docs), while YouTube recommends 2 B-frames. CM4's bcm2835-codec cannot produce B-frames, so this is moot on CM4. On CM5, x264 must run with bframes=0 / tune=zerolatency, and YouTube quality at a given bitrate may drop.

GStreamer v4l2h264enc on BCM2711 reports 0 encoder latency, because bcm2835-codec does not expose MIN_BUFFERS_FOR_CAPTURE to the encoder. Pipeline latency and A/V sync calculations will undercount by the real encode time (about 10-23 ms).

Default GStreamer element latencies can hide hundreds of ms to seconds in the live path: rtspsrc/rtspclientsink 2000 ms, rtpbin/webrtcbin/rtpjitterbuffer 200 ms, and x264enc without tune (frame threads plus lookahead). Each must be set explicitly.

CM5 runs both encodes (recording and live) in software. If x264 cannot finish each frame within 33.3 ms, V4L2/GStreamer FIFO queues grow and add 33.3 ms per queued frame without bound. The live branch needs leaky queues, or a lower live resolution or frame rate.
If ICE falls back to TCP (webrtcLocalTCPAddress) or a TCP TURN relay, MediaMTX documents a 'progressive delay when network is congested'. Internet viewers behind NAT may be forced onto TURN.
Internet viewers need UDP 8189 forwarded and the public IP or DNS name in webrtcAdditionalHosts, or STUN/TURN in webrtcICEServers2. A LAN-only setup will silently fail for remote viewers.
WHEP is still an Internet-Draft (-04, awaiting WG chair go-ahead). MediaMTX's /whep behaviour may change when the RFC is published.

Debian trixie does not package gst-plugins-rs webrtcsink/whipclientsink. A design that relies on them needs a self-built Rust plugin. Publishing RTSP into MediaMTX (the MediaMTX-recommended GStreamer path) avoids this.

The bcm2835-codec default GOP of 60 frames (2 s at 30p) lengthens WebRTC join time (wait for IDR) and stretches HLS segments, because MediaMTX extends segments to include an IDR. A GOP of 2 s or less is also YouTube's recommendation.
LL-HLS on Apple devices requires MediaMTX HTTPS (hlsEncryption), which adds certificate management on an embedded device.
